ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: wishes and promises
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How wishes work, and what granting, promising, refusing and ignoring do.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A promise kept is worth three wishes granted. A promise broken costs more than all three.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists voice wishes that fit their situation, their traits and what the colony can actually build. Each wish has a deadline. Grant it and they're pleased, motivated and trust the council more; let it lapse and it stings. Promising buys patience but raises the stakes; refusing honestly hurts a little now and is over.

facts.li: A granted wish always makes the colonist motivated (faster work for a few days), more so if promised.
The happier a colonist already is, the more likely a granted wish inspires them instead: creativity, a work or shooting frenzy, recruiting, surgery.
Promising adds half the remaining time plus two days, and +4 trust now; breaking it costs far more than an ordinary lapse.
Some wishes act on a promise straight away: promising a party calls one, promising a hunt marks the prey.
Out of patience, colonists sometimes do it themselves: plan the lamp, take the bed, set their own work priorities. They trust the council less for it.
Others react: friends are happy for them, the jealous feel passed over, and some will object out loud.

advice.li: Promise only what you'll actually do in time.
Refuse what you won't do. A clean no beats a lapse.
Watch for wishes that come with objections: granting them pleases one colonist and annoys another.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: trust in the council
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Bitter to devoted: what trust does to mood, work and loyalty.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: People forgive a poor colony. They don't forgive being ignored.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every colonist has a level of trust in the council: bitter, doubtful, neutral, trusting or devoted. It rises with granted wishes, kept promises and heeded petitions, falls with lapses, refusals and broken promises, and slowly drifts back towards neutral. It shows in the Wishes tab, with its history in the tooltip.

facts.li: Trusting and devoted colonists work and learn faster and break less (shown in the health tab as "loyal to the council").
Doubtful and bitter colonists work slower and snap sooner ("grudge against the council").
Trusting colonists are more patient with their wishes; bitter ones less so.

On Demanding stakes, a colonist who stays bitter for days may announce they're leaving, and walk out three days later unless their trust recovers. Children, anyone whose partner stays, and colonies of fewer than four never lose someone this way.
Living under a decree they hate wears trust down day by day; one they love builds it.

advice.li: When someone announces they're leaving, grant one of their wishes or keep a promise: that's usually enough.
Check the trust list before big decisions: it tells you who can take a disappointment and who can't.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: rising standards
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Comfort breeds expectations: why a happy colony gets harder to please.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Feed them fine meals for a season and simple ones start to taste like an insult.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: While a colonist is happy, their standards creep up from modest to comfortable, particular and spoiled. High standards shrink the council's rewards and sharpen its disappointments. Hard times bring them back down, and so does the austerity decree.

facts.li: Standards rise while mood is above about 70%, faster above 85%; ascetics barely rise, the greedy and jealous rise faster.
They fall while mood is below 40%, slowly in between, and quickly under austerity.
Spoiled colonists get half the mood from the council's rewards and about 40% more from its letdowns.
They're less patient, voice wishes more often, reach for luxuries, and ask for more: two impressiveness levels instead of one, fine meals instead of simple ones.
Feasts, festivals and bonfires raise everyone's standards a little.

advice.li: If the whole colony is particular or spoiled, a week of austerity resets expectations cheaply.
Not every celebration has to happen. Saying no now keeps the next yes worth something.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: decrees
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Trade mood for output: long hours, rationing, drills and the rest.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: A happy colony is a colony you can push. Push it before something else does.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The Decrees tab puts policies in force for a few days: up to two at once, each with a cooldown afterwards. Each trades mood (and sometimes trust) for something the colony needs, or, like festival days and days of mourning, the other way round. The tab shows who will love or hate each one before you decide.

facts.li: Long hours: work 15% faster. Rationing: hunger 25% slower. Drills: everyone who can fight trains shooting and melee every waking hour.
Study hours: learning 30% and research 20% faster. Harvest push, building season, clean sweep: faster at one kind of work.
Best behavior: better negotiating, recruiting and trade prices. On guard: better aim and melee, more tiredness.
Austerity: no new wishes, standards fall fast. Festival days: a big mood lift, work much slower, standards rise.
Days of mourning: only while someone grieves; grief fades much faster and nobody breaks as easily.
Colonists sometimes petition for a decree when the moment fits. Declaring it within five days wins their trust.

advice.li: Pair a hated decree with a short one people love, or follow it with festival days.
Ration before winter, not during it. Drill before raids grow, not after.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: dilemmas
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Hard choices where every answer costs someone something.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: There's no right answer. There's only the answer you can live with, and the people who can't.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Every week or so, more often while everyone is content, the council is asked to settle something: a thief, a feud, a stash, a feast, a confession, a duel, the spoils of a raid. A letter lists the answers. Colonists react according to their nature, and some answers are gambles. Answer within the time given, or the council's silence decides.

facts.li: Some answers take real things from the stores: food, wood, silver. They're greyed out if you can't afford them.
Seasonal dilemmas (midsummer, harvest home, the longest night, naming the year) and after-battle ones (the spoils, the enemy dead, a victory feast) come up at their moment.
Every dilemma and its answer is written into the chronicle and counted in the year's annals.

advice.li: Check the trust list first: a colonist who is already doubtful takes being overruled much harder.
When kind colonists and hard ones are both present, the "fair" answer usually upsets fewest.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: names, anniversaries and annals
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: How the colony remembers its people and its years.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Write it down. In a hundred years, the annals are all anyone will know about us.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Whoever has done the most of something earns a name for it (the Healer, Deadeye, the Kindling) until someone overtakes them. Each year since a colonist joined is marked. And when a new year begins, the colony's best reader or talker writes the annals of the year that ended.

facts.li: Names come from the colonist's records: wounds tended, operations, kills, headshots, things built, rock mined, harvests, meals, animals tamed, prisoners recruited, research, crafting, fires fought, and less flattering ones like messes cleaned, times on fire or mental breaks.
A name moves to someone else only when they're clearly ahead (by about 15%).
The annals cover who joined, died, left or walked out, raids, wealth, wishes, ambitions, decrees, dilemmas, friendships, feuds, trust and names. Past years can be reread from the Chronicle tab.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: offices and elections
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: Speaker, marshal, quartermaster, physician, steward: who holds them and what they do.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: The colony votes for who it likes. Sometimes that's even who it needs.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: The council has five seats. Each gives its holder an edge and does a job for the whole colony. Colonists elect them once a year, voting for whoever is good at the job, has the right nature for it, and is liked. The council can appoint or dismiss anyone from the Decrees tab, but overruling the vote has a price.

facts.li: Speaker: chairs every council meeting; everyone's trust rises a little each day.
Marshal: drills train half again as fast; the colony aims and strikes a little better.
Quartermaster: answers to dilemmas that cost food, wood or silver cost a quarter less; better trade prices.
Physician: everyone heals and fights off illness a little faster.
Steward: standards rise a quarter more slowly; the steward gets more out of recreation.
The first election comes after about a week, then one every new year. An empty seat is refilled by a by-election a few days later.
Nobody holds two offices. Children, slaves and lodgers can't stand.
Votes follow skill, traits and friendship: friends and members of the same circle vote for each other, rivals against.
Losing an election or a seat sours the loser on the winner, and can start a rivalry.

advice.li: Appoint over the vote only when the difference matters. The one who was elected will remember.
A good speaker is the cheapest trust you'll ever buy.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: traditions
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What the colony keeps doing becomes expected.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Do something twice and it's a habit. Do it three times and you'll never hear the end of it if you stop.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Some seasonal dilemmas have an answer the colony can make its own: a midsummer feast, a harvest celebration, a vigil on the longest night. Choose the same answer two years running and it becomes a tradition. From then on it comes up first every year, keeping it pleases everyone, and breaking it disappoints them.

facts.li: The letter says when a choice is a tradition, and when choosing it again will make one.
Keeping a tradition gives everyone a good memory; breaking one gives a bad one and resets the count.
New, kept and broken traditions are written into the chronicle and the year's annals, and someone usually writes about a new tradition in their journal.

advice.li: Traditions cost something every year. Only start the ones you can afford in a bad year too.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: friends, rivals, comrades and mentors
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: The bonds between colonists: how they form, grow, sour and end, and what they change.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: You can order people to work together. You can't order them to like it.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: Colonists form lasting bonds out of how they feel about each other and what they go through. Steady liking turns into friendship, steady loathing into rivalry, fighting side by side into comradeship, and a skilled colonist may take an eager learner under their wing. Every bond has a strength and a short history, shown in the Social tab of the council window.

facts.li: Friends and rivals form when two colonists' opinions of each other stay high (or low) enough. A bond then drifts with how they feel, and ends when it fades to nothing.
Everyone who deals real damage in the same battle becomes comrades. Comradeship slowly fades between battles.
A mentor (skill 12+, with a passion) teaches a student (skill 7 or less, with a passion) every day until the student reaches level 11. Both are proud when the student graduates.
Bonds give opinion: new, solid and deep bonds count for more each step.
Small social events happen most days: late talks, pranks, snubs, squabbles, war stories, lessons, contests, gifts, gossip and the odd truce. Each moves the bond a little.
Three or more colonists held together by strong friendships or shared battles form a circle. Colonists outside every circle, with no close friend, sometimes feel left out.

The council's decisions feed back: losing an election to someone, having your wish passed over for theirs, a fight, a grudge from a dilemma or arguing over a decree can start rivalries; backing the same petition, making up or going through something together builds friendships.
Bonds change how people act: friends and circle members back each other's wishes and petitions and vote for each other; rivals object to each other's wishes and vote against each other.
Let someone's wish lapse and their close friends trust the council a little less, the rest of their circle more so.
A colonist's bonds and circle are listed in their trust tooltip in the Wishes tab.
When a bonded colonist dies, the ones left behind write about it.

advice.li: Two rivals on the same work shift is a squabble waiting to happen. Two friends on a raid is a comradeship waiting to happen.
Want a skill to survive a death? Look for a mentorship in the Social tab, or make sure a passionate learner works next to your best.
A strong circle is a voting bloc. Keep its members happy, or they'll be unhappy together.

ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.label: dreams
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.summary: What colonists dream about, and the rare dream that changes something or comes true.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.tip: Ask them what they dreamt. You'll learn more than from a month of work reports.
ColonyCouncil.AlmanacArticleDef.description: A colonist who sleeps (or lies unconscious) for four hours or more may wake from a dream. Dreams grow out of their life: the battle two days ago, the friend they lost, the rival who insulted them, the wish the council ignored, the leg they no longer have, the skill they're learning. Most dreams are just a passing mood and a line in their journal. Hover the mood in their needs tab to read the dream itself.

facts.li: Dreams about what really happened (a raid, a death, an insult, a broken promise, an illness, an addiction) are far more likely than others. Unhappy colonists have more nightmares, and volatile ones more still.
People in their lives turn up: friends, rivals, partners, family, comrades, teachers and students, bonded animals, and the dead they loved.

Now and then a dream changes something: an inspiration, a lesson in a skill, a good night's rest, a nightmare that leaves them shaken, a dream of a won fight that steadies their aim, a softened rivalry, a wish.
Rarely, a dream is an omen, and a few days later it comes true: a caravan, a newcomer, falling cargo pods, a cold snap, a raid. Only one omen waits at a time. You can turn omens off in the settings.
Colonists tell each other their dreams. Telling someone you dreamt about them makes them like you a little more.
Recent dreams are listed at the bottom of the Social tab, and dreams that came true go in the chronicle and the year's annals.

advice.li: When a colonist wakes up talking about torches in the dark, check your defenses. It costs nothing.
A colonist with recurring nightmares is telling you something about their life. Look at their mood.
